item.title: Governing urban circular economy transitions: A mechanism-informed heuristic for local government
item.description:
Roelof Vogel, Martin Geissdoerfer, Glen Croy, Amrik Sohal
European Urban and Regional Studies
DOI: 10.1177/09697764261496822
Despite the recognised role of the urban circular economy as a pathway to sustainable development within global planetary boundaries, governance of circular economy transitions by local government remains poorly operationalised. Existing sustainability transition frameworks provide theoretical perspectives but are insufficiently place-based, underspecify the role of actors and agency and have not been integrated into a coherent governance process for local government. Drawing on 65 semi-structured interviews with actors across government, business and knowledge providers, complemented by policy document analysis, we compare three local governments in each of metropolitan Amsterdam (The Netherlands) and metropolitan Melbourne (Australia) to contrast the respective stages of implementation maturity. Following a retrodictive analytical logic, we develop three candidate explanatory mechanisms for circular economy governance: (i) a ‘legitimation’ mechanism, whereby multilevel policy alignment reduces institutional risk within the circular ecosystem; (ii) a ‘boundary-spanning’ mechanism through which local government officers bridge between entrepreneurial and public-governance institutional logics and (iii) a ‘competitive-displacement mechanism’ whereby cooperative actor relationships shift toward competition as circular economy solutions mature toward mainstream adoption. Grounded in these mechanisms, we propose a three-step heuristic model, comprising (1) contextual ecosystem analysis, (2) intervention strategy development and (3) transition management. We introduce a circular ecosystem framework for place-specific actor mapping to operationalise the process. We present the mechanisms as a bounded middle-range explanation and the model as context-sensitive guidance, rather than as a deterministic or universally predictive account.
